source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: 1905, Charles Scribner's Sons (serialized in Scribner's Magazine from January 1905)

source.excerpt: "That's unjust, I think, because, as I understand it, one of the conditions of citizenship is not to think too much about money, and the only way not to think about money is to have a great deal of it." "You might as well say that the only way not to think about air is to have enough to breathe."
trail: First published in 1905 by Charles Scribner's Sons; the full novel text is hosted at Project Gutenberg.
The exact sentence is confirmed verbatim, in context, on Wikisource's Chapter 6.
Wikiquote lists this quote, sourced to Book I, Chapter 6, in its verified (non-misattributed) quotes section.
source.excerptNote: Dialogue between Lily Bart and Lawrence Selden.
source.rightsNote: The House of Mirth was first published in 1905, well before the 1928/1931 U.S. public-domain cutoff, so the novel — and this line from it — is in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: Edith Wharton
author.heading: About Edith Wharton
author.metaLine: 1862–1937 · American novelist, first woman to win the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction
author.bio: Edith Wharton drew on her insider's knowledge of Gilded Age New York society to write incisive, often satirical novels of manners, including The House of Mirth (1905), Ethan Frome (1911), and The Age of Innocence, for which she won the 1921 Pulitzer Prize. Her fiction repeatedly probes how money and social convention trap her characters, especially women.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The quote is genuinely Wharton's, but two smaller distortions circulate online.

items.why: Some quotation pages render the line as "The only way to not think about money…" rather than Wharton's actual "the only way not to think about money…" — confirmed by comparing the Goodreads version against the original text.

At least one print-on-demand reprint uses this line as a marketing subtitle on the cover of Wharton's later, unrelated novel The Glimpses of the Moon. The full text of that novel, checked directly on Project Gutenberg, does not contain the line at all; it belongs solely to The House of Mirth (1905).

misattribution.truthLine: The line is genuine Wharton dialogue from The House of Mirth, Book I, Chapter 6, spoken by the character Lily Bart — and immediately rebutted within the same scene by another character.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line is not Wharton's own aphorism offered in her own voice — it is dialogue given to Lily Bart, the beautiful but financially precarious heroine of The House of Mirth, during a bantering exchange with Lawrence Selden about whether she could ever be truly happy among the "idle rich."

Selden immediately punctures Lily's line with a rejoinder — "You might as well say that the only way not to think about air is to have enough to breathe" — making clear the novel treats the sentiment as a clever but self-deceiving rationalization, not a moral endorsed by the author.
context.pull: "...the only way not to think about money is to have a great deal of it."
